title: You probably would have walked past him.
paragraphs: You probably would have walked past him.
A grown man lying on his side… day after day… silent, restrained, staring toward a city that hadn’t even fallen yet.
People mocked him. Some pitied him. Others just shook their heads and moved on.
But heaven wasn’t confused.
God was speaking—loudly.
And almost no one was listening.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior

In the Book of Ezekiel, chapter 4 opens with something that feels almost uncomfortable to read. God commands Ezekiel to lie on his left side for 390 days… then on his right side for 40 days. Not hours. Not symbolic minutes. Days.
“Lie also on your left side, and lay the iniquity of the house of Israel upon it… For I have laid upon thee the years of their iniquity, according to the number of the days…” (Ezekiel 4:4–5)
Read that again.
God was turning a man into a living message.
Every day Ezekiel stayed on that side, he was carrying—visibly—the weight of Israel’s rebellion. Three hundred ninety years of sin represented in his stillness. Then forty more for Judah.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
This wasn’t just about numbers.
It was about exposure.
Israel had been sinning for generations—quietly, culturally, comfortably. Idolatry wasn’t shocking anymore. Disobedience had become normal. They still had religion… but they had lost God.
And God said, “If you won’t hear My words… you will see them.”
So Ezekiel became the message.
Bound. Restricted. Unable to turn freely.
Just like them.

You say you’re free… but your habits say otherwise.
You say you love God… but your life leans another direction.
You say it’s not that serious…

God saw it.
You knew.
Ezekiel lying there wasn’t random. It was a mirror.
Israel was spiritually paralyzed. Stuck in sin they refused to confront. Unable—no, unwilling—to turn back to God.
So God showed them what they had become.
And then it gets heavier.
God tells Ezekiel to face Jerusalem while lying there… to prophesy against it… while rationing food and water like someone under siege.
Because judgment was coming.
Not maybe.
Not someday.
It was already set in motion.

You think ignoring sin delays consequences.
It doesn’t.
It stores them.
“For the wages of sin is death…” (Romans 6:23)
That hasn’t changed.
But here’s where everything shifts.
Because Ezekiel was lying on his side… but he wasn’t the only one who would carry sin.
Centuries later, another Man would come—not to symbolize sin… but to take it.
“And the Lord hath laid on Him the iniquity of us all.” (Isaiah 53:6)
Jesus didn’t lie on His side.
He hung on a cross.
Not for 390 days… not for 40 days…
But once—fully, completely, eternally.
Where Ezekiel carried a picture of judgment, Jesus carried the full weight of it.
Where Ezekiel was bound as a sign, Jesus was nailed as a substitute.
That’s the difference.
Ezekiel showed what sin does.
Jesus finished what sin demands.
So now the question isn’t whether sin is serious.
You already know that.
The question is… what are you doing with what God has shown you?

You can normalize what God calls rebellion.
You can stay where you are.
Or…
You can finally turn.
Repentance isn’t dramatic on the outside. It’s decisive on the inside.

It’s the moment you stop pretending you’re not stuck.
It’s the moment you stop negotiating with sin.
It’s the moment you stop delaying obedience.
“Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out…” (Acts 3:19)
There are only two directions from here.
Stay as you are… comfortable, familiar, slowly hardening.
Or turn toward Christ… where grace doesn’t ignore sin—but destroys its power.
If something in you feels exposed right now… don’t bury it.
That’s not guilt for shame.
That’s conviction calling you back.
Say it plainly if it’s real:
“I’ve been stuck… and I need Jesus.”
Write it. Don’t hide it.
Follow if you’re done with surface-level faith and want truth that actually changes you.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—not just hearing truth, but growing in it, being sharpened, corrected, built—step into it here:
This isn’t about information.
It’s about transformation.
